a: to look the other way
p: The Greek and a Dead Sea scroll read "a pair of sandals? Testify against me!" where the Hebrew has "to hide my eyes with it."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930); Targum; Vulgate
readings.en: and I hid my eyes with it
readings.plain: to look the other way

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek), Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD); 4QSam-a (Dead Sea Scrolls, about 50–25 BC), partly preserved and partly reconstructed in DJD 17; compare Sirach 46:19
readings.en: or a sandal? Answer against me
readings.plain: or even a pair of sandals? Testify against me

why: The two readings come from almost the same Hebrew letters (w'lm 'yny bw and n'lym 'nw by). The Masoretic reading makes clear sense, so the Plain English Translation follows it, but the Greek reading is old and may be original.
b: The difference is a matter of a few letters. Read one way, Samuel asks whether he took a bribe "to hide my eyes" from justice. Read the other way, he asks whether he took even "a pair of sandals," a small bribe (compare Amos 2:6; Amos 8:6, where the poor are sold "for a pair of sandals"). The Wisdom of Ben Sira, written about 180 BC, remembers Samuel's words in the second form: before his death he testified that he had not taken anyone's goods, "not even a pair of sandals" (Sirach 46:19). So this reading was known in Hebrew in Jerusalem about 140 years before 4QSam-a was copied.

a: Barak
p: The Hebrew names an unknown judge, Bedan. The Greek and Syriac read Barak, the judge who fought with Deborah.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930); Vulgate
readings.plain: Bedan

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek), Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD); Syriac Peshitta
readings.plain: Barak

why: No judge named Bedan is known, and Barak fits the order of Judges (Jerubbaal = Gideon, Barak, Jephthah). The letters of the two names are close in Hebrew script.
b: A Bedan appears only in a list of Manasseh's descendants (1 Chronicles 7:17). The rabbis said Bedan was Samson, reading the name as ben Dan, "the son of Dan," since Samson was a Danite (Rosh Hashanah 25a), and Rashi follows them. Most modern translations follow the Greek and Syriac and read Barak. In Hebrew script the d of Bedan and the r of Barak are easily confused; the last letters (n and q) are not, so the change was not a simple slip of one letter. Hebrews 11:32 lists "Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David and Samuel," a list that may reflect the same tradition.

a: Samuel
p: Would Samuel name himself in a list of rescuers? Some Greek manuscripts and the Syriac read Samson.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930); Septuagint (Old Greek), Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD)
readings.plain: Samuel

readings.w: Septuagint (Lucianic manuscripts); Syriac Peshitta
readings.plain: Samson

why: "Samuel" has the best support, and the Plain English Translation keeps it. Samuel speaking of himself in the third person is unusual but possible in a solemn speech.
b: It sounds odd for Samuel to end his list of judges with his own name. Some readers think a scribe changed Samson to Samuel because Samson's story ends badly; others that a scribe changed Samuel to Samson to avoid the oddity. Samuel did rescue Israel at Mizpah (7:10–13), so the name fits the history. The Targum and the rabbis, who already read "Bedan" as Samson, kept "Samuel" here.

a: and on your ancestors
p: The Hebrew warns that the LORD's hand will be against "you and your fathers." The Greek reads "you and your king."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930)
readings.plain: and on your ancestors

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek), Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD)
readings.plain: and on your king

why: The Hebrew is harder, since the ancestors are dead, and so is probably older. The Plain English Translation translates it as it stands.
b: The Greek fits the speech, which twice pairs "you and your king" (12:14; 12:25). But that is exactly why a scribe might have made the change. Many translations smooth the Hebrew into a comparison, as the KJV did: "as it was against your fathers." Others take "your ancestors" to mean the ancestral line, Israel as a whole across the generations.

a: Saul was [...] years old when he became king. He ruled over Israel [...] two years.
p: The Hebrew says Saul was "a year old" and reigned "two years." Numbers have dropped out of the text.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930)
readings.orig: בֶּן־שָׁנָה שָׁאוּל בְּמָלְכוֹ וּשְׁתֵּי שָׁנִים מָלַךְ עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵל
readings.en: Saul was a son of a year when he reigned, and two years he reigned over Israel
readings.plain: Saul was [...] years old when he became king. He ruled over Israel [...] two years.

readings.w: Septuagint (some Lucianic manuscripts and a Hexaplaric note)
readings.plain: Saul was thirty years old when he became king. He ruled over Israel [...] two years.

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek), Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD)

why: This verse follows the standard formula for a king's age and reign (2 Samuel 2:10; 2 Samuel 5:4), but both numbers are broken. The Plain English Translation marks the gaps rather than guess.
b: Literally the Hebrew says "Saul was a son of a year when he reigned." The word for the age seems to be missing, as if the scribe had a blank in his source. "Thirty" in some Greek manuscripts is likely a guess. Jonathan is already a commander (13:2), so Saul was probably over forty. The second number, "two years," may be the end of a larger number, such as twenty-two or thirty-two. Acts 13:21 says Saul reigned forty years, and Josephus gives different figures in different places. The rabbis read the Hebrew as "Saul was as innocent as a one-year-old" (Yoma 22b; Targum). Some English versions fill in thirty and forty-two; the Plain English Translation shows where the gap is.

a: Let the Hebrews hear!
p: In the Greek, Saul proclaims "The slaves have revolted!" Some scholars move the cry to the Philistines.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930)
readings.plain: Let the Hebrews hear!

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek), Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD)
readings.orig: καὶ Σαουλ σάλπιγγι σαλπίζει εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν λέγων Ἠθετήκασιν οἱ δοῦλοι
readings.en: and Saul blows the trumpet in all the land, saying, The slaves have revolted
readings.plain: The slaves have revolted!

why: The Hebrew is clear enough, and the Plain English Translation follows it. The Greek reading may come from a Hebrew text with similar letters (pash'u ha'avadim).
b: In the Greek, as in the Hebrew, Saul sounds the horn and makes the proclamation; only his words differ. "The slaves have revolted" would announce that Israel has thrown off Philistine rule. Some modern scholars (Wellhausen, McCarter) go further and reconstruct the original so that the Philistines say "The Hebrews have revolted," since "Hebrews" is the word foreigners use for Israelites in these chapters (13:19; 14:11). The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.

a: three thousand chariots
p: The Hebrew says thirty thousand chariots, far more than any ancient army had. Some Greek manuscripts and the Syriac read three thousand.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930); Septuagint (Old Greek), Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD)
readings.plain: thirty thousand chariots

readings.w: Septuagint (Lucianic manuscripts); Syriac Peshitta
readings.plain: three thousand chariots

why: Thirty thousand chariots is not believable for the Philistines; even the great empires fielded a few thousand. The smaller number is likely original, the larger perhaps a copying slip.
b: At the Battle of Qarqar (853 BC), the largest chariot army we know of in the region, Ahab of Israel brought 2,000 chariots. Thirty thousand would also be out of proportion to six thousand horsemen. A scribe may have repeated the last letter of the word "Israel" before the number (l, which could stand for thirty), turning three into thirty. Most modern translations follow the smaller number.

a: going up to Gibeah in Benjamin
p: The Greek has an extra sentence explaining how Saul and the troops got from Gilgal to Gibeah.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930)
readings.en: and he went up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin
readings.plain: going up to Gibeah in Benjamin

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek), Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD)
readings.orig: καὶ ἀνέστη Σαμουηλ καὶ ἀπῆλθεν ἐκ Γαλγαλων εἰς ὁδὸν αὐτοῦ. καὶ τὸ κατάλειμμα τοῦ λαοῦ ἀνέβη ὀπίσω Σαουλ εἰς ἀπάντησιν ὀπίσω τοῦ λαοῦ τοῦ πολεμιστοῦ. αὐτῶν παραγενομένων ἐκ Γαλγαλων εἰς Γαβαα Βενιαμιν
readings.en: and Samuel arose and went away from Gilgal on his way. And the rest of the people went up after Saul to meet the people of war. When they came from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin
readings.plain: going on his way. The rest of the people went up after Saul to meet the fighting men, and they came from Gilgal to Gibeah in Benjamin

why: The Greek may preserve words the Hebrew lost when a scribe's eye jumped from one "from Gilgal" to the next. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew but the Greek is a real possibility.
b: In the Hebrew, Samuel goes to Gibeah, and then Saul is suddenly at Gibeah with his troops (13:16). The Greek explains: Samuel went his own way, and Saul and the people went from Gilgal to Gibeah. Both phrases contain "from Gilgal," so a skip from the first to the second would remove the sentence in between. Many scholars (McCarter, Klein) accept the Greek.

a: his sickle
p: The Hebrew repeats the word for the first tool, "plowshare." The Greek reads "sickle."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930)
readings.en: his plowshare (the same word as the first tool, with different vowels)
readings.plain: his plowshare

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek), Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD)
readings.plain: his sickle

why: Four different tools are clearly meant, and the Hebrew repeats a word, probably by a copying slip. The Plain English Translation follows the Greek. The KJV has "mattock."
b: The Hebrew list is machareshet, et, qardom and machareshah: the first and last are forms of the same word. The next verse names a different set of tools again, so the exact list is uncertain.

a: Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring the ark of God here." At that time the ark of God was with the Israelites.
p: The Hebrew says Saul called for the ark. The Greek says the ephod, which was used to ask God questions.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930)
readings.en: bring near the ark of God
readings.plain: Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring the ark of God here." At that time the ark of God was with the Israelites.

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek), Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD)
readings.orig: προσάγαγε τὸ εφουδ ... ὅτι αὐτὸς ἦρεν τὸ εφουδ
readings.en: bring the ephod ... for he was carrying the ephod
readings.plain: Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring the ephod here." At that time he was carrying the ephod in front of Israel.

why: The Plain English Translation keeps the harder Hebrew reading. But many scholars prefer the Greek, since the ark was at Kiriath-jearim (7:1–2) and Ahijah is said to carry the ephod (14:3).
b: The two Hebrew words, aron (ark) and efod (ephod), are not similar, but the Greek fits the story: Saul wants to ask God whether to attack, then stops the priest in the middle ("Pull back your hand," 14:19), which suits the ephod with its lots. The ark had stayed at Kiriath-jearim since its return (7:1–2) until David brought it to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6). On the other hand, a scribe who knew the ark was elsewhere might have changed "ark" to "ephod," and the ark could be taken to battle (4:3–4; 2 Samuel 11:11).

a: That day the men of Israel were hard pressed.
p: The Greek has a longer verse: Saul "committed a great act of ignorance" with his oath.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930)
readings.en: and the men of Israel were hard pressed that day
readings.plain: That day the men of Israel were hard pressed.

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek), Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD)
readings.orig: καὶ Σαουλ ἠγνόησεν ἄγνοιαν μεγάλην ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ
readings.en: and Saul committed a great error on that day
readings.plain: That day Saul made a great blunder.

why: The Hebrew makes sense as it stands. The Greek may come from a Hebrew text that differed in a few letters, or may be a translator's judgment on Saul's oath.
b: The Greek also adds to the end of 14:23 that "all the people were with Saul, about ten thousand men, and the battle spread out into every town in the hill country of Ephraim." Its version of 14:24 then blames Saul directly. In the Hebrew, the people are "hard pressed" because of the battle, or because of the hunger Saul's oath causes. Jonathan's own judgment comes a few verses later (14:29–30).

a: Saul said, "LORD God of Israel, why did you not answer your servant today? If the wrong lies in me or in my son Jonathan, LORD God of Israel, let Urim come out. If the wrong lies in your people Israel, let Thummim come out." Jonathan and Saul were taken by the lot, and the people went free.
p: The Greek and Latin have a longer prayer that names the Urim and Thummim. The Hebrew has "Give tamim."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930)
readings.orig: וַיֹּאמֶר שָׁאוּל אֶל־יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הָבָה תָמִים
readings.en: and Saul said to the LORD God of Israel, Give perfect (tamim)
readings.plain: Saul said to the LORD God of Israel, "Give a perfect answer." Jonathan and Saul were taken by the lot, and the people went free.

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek), Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD); Latin Vulgate
readings.orig: ἐὰν ἐν ἐμοὶ ἢ ἐν Ιωναθαν τῷ υἱῷ μου ἡ ἀδικία, κύριε ὁ θεὸς Ισραηλ, δὸς δήλους· καὶ ἐὰν τάδε εἴπῃς Ἐν τῷ λαῷ σου Ισραηλ, δὸς δὴ ὁσιότητα
readings.en: if the guilt is in me or in Jonathan my son, LORD God of Israel, give Urim; and if it is in your people Israel, give holiness (Thummim)
readings.plain: Saul said, "LORD God of Israel, why did you not answer your servant today? If the wrong lies in me or in my son Jonathan, LORD God of Israel, let Urim come out. If the wrong lies in your people Israel, let Thummim come out." Jonathan and Saul were taken by the lot, and the people went free.

why: The longer text explains how the lot worked and is the only place in the Bible that shows Urim and Thummim in use. The shorter Hebrew is best explained as an accident: a scribe's eye skipped from the first "Israel" to the third, and what was left (tummim) was read as tamim, "perfect."
b: The Greek dēlous ("clear ones") matches the usual Greek rendering of Urim (dēlōsis, Exodus 28:30). For Thummim the Greek here has hosiotēta ("holiness"), which is unusual; elsewhere it is normally alētheia, "truth" (Exodus 28:30; Deuteronomy 33:8). Most modern translations follow the long text (NRSV, NAB, NJB; NJPS in a note). A few defend the Hebrew. The long version shows a yes-or-no procedure: one stone means the guilt is in Saul's family, the other means it is in the people. See the topic on Urim and Thummim.

a: "Now make it fall between me and Jonathan my son," Saul said.
p: The Greek has a longer scene: Saul says whoever the lot takes must die, the people object, and Saul overrules them.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930)
readings.orig: וַיֹּאמֶר שָׁאוּל הַפִּילוּ בֵּינִי וּבֵין יוֹנָתָן בְּנִי
readings.en: and Saul said, Cast between me and Jonathan my son
readings.plain: "Now make it fall between me and Jonathan my son," Saul said.

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek), Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD)
readings.orig: Βάλετε ἀνὰ μέσον ἐμοῦ καὶ ἀνὰ μέσον Ιωναθαν τοῦ υἱοῦ μου· ὃν ἂν κατακληρώσηται κύριος, ἀποθανέτω. καὶ εἶπεν ὁ λαὸς πρὸς Σαουλ Οὐκ ἔστιν τὸ ῥῆμα τοῦτο. καὶ κατεκράτησεν Σαουλ τοῦ λαοῦ
readings.en: Cast between me and Jonathan my son: whomever the Lord takes by lot, let him die. And the people said to Saul, This shall not be. And Saul prevailed over the people
readings.plain: "Now make it fall between me and Jonathan my son," Saul said. "Whoever the LORD takes by the lot must die." The people said to Saul, "This must not happen!" But Saul overruled the people.

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew. The Greek plus may be original, lost together with the words skipped in 14:41, or it may be a later expansion that anticipates the people's protest in 14:45.
b: The plus sharpens the theme of king against people that runs through the chapter: the people protest once and are overruled, then protest again after the lot and win (14:45). Some translations follow it (NAB, NJB). Since the Hebrew of 14:41 has clearly lost words by a scribe's skip, many scholars think this passage may have been lost in the same damaged stretch of text; others see it as an addition.

a: he got the better of them
p: The Hebrew verb usually means "condemn" or "act wickedly." The Greek reads "he was saved."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930)
readings.en: he declared guilty, put in the wrong
readings.plain: he got the better of them

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek), Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD)
readings.en: he was saved, he came out safe
readings.plain: he came out safe

why: The Plain English Translation reads the Hebrew in the sense "put in the wrong," that is, defeated. The Greek may come from yiwwashea, "he was saved," a word with similar letters, and many scholars prefer it.
b: The verb hirshia normally means "to condemn" in a law court. Applied to a war, it may mean Saul "proved them wrong" by defeating them. The KJV has "he vexed them." The Greek reading, "he was victorious" or "delivered," fits Saul's other successes and the word "rescued" in 14:48.

a: Then he moved on and went down to Gilgal.
p: The Greek adds that Saul turned his chariot, and that Saul was found offering burnt offerings from the plunder of Amalek.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930)
readings.en: and he turned and passed on and went down to Gilgal
readings.plain: Then he moved on and went down to Gilgal.

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek), Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD)
readings.orig: καὶ ἐπέστρεψεν τὸ ἅρμα καὶ κατέβη εἰς Γαλγαλα πρὸς Σαουλ, καὶ ἰδοὺ αὐτὸς ἀνέφερεν ὁλοκαύτωσιν τῷ κυρίῳ τὰ πρῶτα τῶν σκύλων ὧν ἤνεγκεν ἐξ Αμαληκ
readings.en: and he turned his chariot and went down to Gilgal to Saul, and look, he was offering a burnt offering to the Lord, the first of the plunder he had brought from Amalek
readings.plain: He turned his chariot and went down to Gilgal. Samuel came down to Saul, and look, he was offering a burnt offering to the LORD, the first of the plunder he had brought from Amalek.

why: The Greek may preserve a line lost from the Hebrew, or may be an explanation drawn from 15:15 and 15:21. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: The Greek's "to Saul" after Gilgal makes it most natural to read Samuel as the one going down, so the Greek has Samuel arrive and catch Saul in the act of sacrificing. It also gives Saul a chariot, the mark of a king (8:11). "The first of the plunder" is stronger than "the best": it uses the language of firstfruits, as if Saul were giving God his share of banned goods that belonged wholly to God. That sharpens Samuel's reply that obeying is better than sacrifice (15:22). The Hebrew leaves Saul's sacrifice as his own explanation (15:15; 15:21).

a: Israel's Enduring One does not lie and does not regret
p: The Greek reads "Israel will be split in two," a forecast of the divided kingdom, where the Hebrew names God "the Enduring One of Israel."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930)
readings.orig: וְגַם נֵצַח יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יְשַׁקֵּר וְלֹא יִנָּחֵם
readings.en: and also the Enduring One of Israel will not lie and will not regret
readings.plain: Israel's Enduring One does not lie and does not regret

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek), Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD)
readings.orig: καὶ διαιρεθήσεται Ισραηλ εἰς δύο, καὶ οὐκ ἀποστρέψει οὐδὲ μετανοήσει
readings.en: and Israel will be divided in two, and he will not turn back nor repent
readings.plain: Israel will be split in two. He will not turn back and will not regret

why: The Hebrew title netsach Yisrael is unusual but makes sense, and the Greek seems to read the letters differently, perhaps as a form of chatsah, "divide." The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: The Greek turns the verse into a prophecy of the split between Israel and Judah after Solomon (1 Kings 12), continuing the image of the torn robe (15:27–28). The Hebrew makes the verse a statement about God's character, which is what makes it hard to fit with 15:11 and 15:35, where God does "regret." See the note on 15:29 and the topic on God's regret.

a: Agag came to him in chains. Agag said, "Surely the bitter taste of death has passed."
p: Did Agag come cheerfully, trembling, or in chains? And did he think death had passed, or that death is bitter?

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930)
readings.en: in fetters (or: delightedly) ... surely the bitterness of death has turned aside
readings.plain: Agag came to him in chains. Agag said, "Surely the bitter taste of death has passed."

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek), Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD)
readings.orig: τρέμων ... Εἰ οὕτως πικρὸς ὁ θάνατος;
readings.plain: Agag came to him trembling. Agag said, "Is death really this bitter?"

why: The Hebrew ma'adannot is a rare word: "delicately, cheerfully" (KJV) or "in fetters" (compare Job 38:31). The Plain English Translation takes "in chains" and keeps the Hebrew's words about death.
b: The Hebrew Agag thinks he has been spared: the bitterness of death has passed. The Greek Agag is afraid and cries out that death is bitter. The Greek lacks the verb sar ("has turned aside"), which in Hebrew looks like the first letters of the next word, mar ("bitter"), so one text may have doubled or dropped it. Either way, Samuel's reply follows at once.

a: four cubits and a span
p: The oldest Hebrew manuscript, the Old Greek and Josephus say four cubits and a span (about 6 ft 9 in, or 2 m). The standard Hebrew says six cubits and a span (about 9 ft 9 in).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930); Codex Alexandrinus and some later Greek manuscripts; Targum; Vulgate; Syriac Peshitta
readings.plain: six cubits and a span

readings.w: 4QSam-a (Dead Sea Scrolls, about 50–25 BC); Old Greek (Codex Vaticanus; Lucianic text); Josephus, Antiquities 6.171 (AD 93–94)
readings.orig: ארבע אמות וזרת; τεσσάρων πήχεων καὶ σπιθαμῆς
readings.plain: four cubits and a span

why: Three old and partly independent witnesses agree on four, and numbers tend to grow in copying. The Plain English Translation follows the Greek here for the same reason it does at 13:5: the larger number is the less likely one. The NET Bible also reads four.
b:
A cubit was about 18 inches (45 cm), a span about 9 inches (23 cm). Four cubits and a span makes Goliath about 6 feet 9 inches, very tall at a time when men averaged about 5 feet 6 inches. Six cubits and a span is nearly 10 feet, taller than any human reliably measured.

Daniel Hays argues for four: the scroll 4QSam-a, the Old Greek and Josephus (who used a Greek text close to the scroll) agree, and a scribe could easily have raised four to six under the influence of "six hundred shekels" in 17:7 or the six-fingered giant of 2 Samuel 21:20. Clyde Billington defends six. He argues that the Alexandrian translators converted Goliath's height into the larger royal (Egyptian) cubit, giving a lower number for the same height, and that 4QSam-a was corrected toward the Greek or copied by someone using that system. He also notes that Codex Alexandrinus and some other Greek manuscripts read six. Hays answers that there is no evidence the translators converted measures anywhere else, and that Alexandrinus was revised toward the Hebrew.

Both sides agree the story does not depend on the number: Goliath was a big man in heavy armor against a youth, and Saul, a head taller than anyone in Israel (10:23), would not face him.

a: David was the son of that Ephrathite from Bethlehem in Judah whose name was Jesse. Jesse had eight sons. In the days of Saul, he was an old man, well on in years.
p: The oldest Greek text lacks 17:12–31, and much more of chapters 17–18. Was there once a shorter story of David and Goliath?

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008; Aleppo Codex, about AD 930); later Greek manuscripts (Codex Alexandrinus, Lucianic text); Targum; Vulgate; Syriac Peshitta
readings.en: and David was the son of this Ephrathite
readings.plain: David was the son of that Ephrathite from Bethlehem in Judah whose name was Jesse. Jesse had eight sons. In the days of Saul, he was an old man, well on in years.

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek), Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD), with some related Greek manuscripts

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text, the received text of the synagogue and the church, but whether the shorter Greek represents an earlier form of the story is one of the most debated questions in the textual study of the Hebrew Bible.
b:
The oldest form of the Greek translation, found in Codex Vaticanus and a few related manuscripts, lacks about 44 percent of 1 Samuel 17–18: by Emanuel Tov's count, 39 of the 88 verses. It lacks 17:12–31 (David arrives at the camp), 17:41, 17:48b, 17:50, 17:55–18:5 (Saul asks whose son David is; Jonathan's covenant), 18:10–11 (the first spear), 18:17–19 (Merab), 18:29b–30, and smaller pieces of 18:6, 18:8, 18:12, 18:21, 18:26 and 18:27, each with its own entry. Later Greek manuscripts, such as Codex Alexandrinus and the Lucianic text, have these passages, added from a Hebrew-based revision.

Read on its own, the short text tells one smooth story. David, already Saul's armor-bearer (16:21), volunteers to fight the Philistine, is armed by Saul, and kills him. Read on its own, the longer material tells another: David, an unknown shepherd boy sent with food for his brothers, hears the challenge, kills the giant, and is then introduced to Saul, who does not know him (17:55–58).

Scholars explain this in two main ways. Emanuel Tov and Johan Lust argue that the Greek translates a shorter Hebrew text, and that the Masoretic Text combined it with a second, independent version of the story. The translator of Samuel usually follows his Hebrew closely, they point out, so he is unlikely to have cut almost half of two chapters. Dominique Barthélemy and D. W. Gooding argue that the long Hebrew is one carefully built story, and that the Greek translator, or the Hebrew text he used, cut passages to remove what seemed contradictions. Gooding's strongest point is that the short text is still not smooth: David is still a "lad" who has never fought (17:33; 17:42) although 16:18 called him "a strong fighter and a soldier," so the shortening did not remove every tension, and the long text's repetitions can be read as deliberate design. The four scholars set out their views together in The Story of David and Goliath (1986).

Since then more specialists have sided with Tov and Lust than with Barthélemy and Gooding; A. Graeme Auld and Craig Ho, for example, argue that the longer text was built up from the shorter. The question remains open. Benjamin Johnson's literary study (2015) reads the Greek version as a coherent story in its own right, a reminder that each text can be read on its own terms. Harmonizing readers (H) read the long text as one story: David served Saul part-time (17:15), Saul asked about his family, not his name (17:25; 17:58), and the narrator arranged events by theme rather than strict time. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text, which is the canonical text for Jews and most Christians, and marks every verse that the Old Greek lacks.

readings.orig: καὶ προσέθετο ἔτι Ιωναθαν ὀμόσαι τῷ Δαυιδ
readings.en: and Jonathan again swore to David
readings.plain: Jonathan swore to David once more

why: Both make sense. In the Hebrew Jonathan, who has just asked for loyalty to his family (20:14–15), binds David to it; in the Greek he binds himself.
b: The difference is one vowel pattern in Hebrew (lehashbia', "to make swear," against lishshava', "to swear"). Jonathan has the greater power now, but David will have it later, which is why Jonathan wants David's oath.

why: No stone Ezel is known, but the Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew. The Greek seems to read ha'argov ("the mound, heap of stones"), which also appears in 20:41.
b: Some have explained Ezel as "departure," a stone of parting. Many scholars read the Greek in both places: David hides beside a mound of stones and gets up from beside it (20:41).

b: If the Greek is right, 20:19 and 20:41 both mention the same mound of stones where David hid. The Hebrew may have lost the place-name and supplied a direction instead.
